title: De motu vibratorio laminarum elasticarum, ubi plures novae vibrationum species hactenus non pertractatae evolvuntur

deep.reconstruction:
Context: Problem II of E443 treats a uniform elastic lamina (Euler–Bernoulli beam) that is free at end A and pinned by a stylus at end B, so it can turn freely about B. Separating variables gives y = A cos φ + B sin φ + C e^φ + D e^{-φ}, with φ = θx/b. The conditions at B are zero bending moment and y = 0. With the free-end conditions at A already built in, the previous page reduces these to the frequency equation tan ζ = tanh ζ, where ζ = θa/b. Euler also writes it as e^{2ζ} = tan(½ϱ + ζ), where ϱ denotes a right angle, π/2.

On this page:
(1) ζ = 0 is a root. Euler calls it the state of equilibrium; physically it is the zero-frequency mode, a rigid rotation about the pin.
(2) The nonzero roots approach (4n+1)π/4, written 5/2 ϱ, 9/2 ϱ, 13/2 ϱ, ….
(3) For the first root he sets ζ = 5π/4 − ω. Then tan ζ = (1 − tan ω)/(1 + tan ω) ≈ (1 − ω)/(1 + ω), while tanh ζ = (1 − e^{−2ζ})/(1 + e^{−2ζ}). Matching the two gives ω = e^{−2ζ} = e^{2ω}/e^{5π/2}.
(4) First approximation: ω ≈ e^{−5π/2} = 0.0003882. One fixed-point iteration gives 0.0003885. Both are correct.
(5) For the higher roots the correction e^{−(4n+1)π/2} is negligible, so ζ ≈ 9π/4 = 7.06858, 13π/4 = 10.21017, 17π/4 = 13.35176.
(6) The substitution ζ → −η leaves the equation invariant, so negative roots mirror the positive ones and give the same θθ.

The next page converts the roots into periods (∝ π/ζ²) and pitches (∝ ζ²/π), and compares them with the free–free and clamped cases. Mathematically this is the free–pinned beam, whose roots are the same as those of the clamped–pinned beam: 3.9266, 7.0686, 10.2102, 13.3518.
errors: The printed value I. ζ = 3.92666 is wrong in the 5th decimal. With 5π/4 = 3.9269908 and ω = 0.0003885, ζ = 3.9266023, which is also the true root of tan ζ = tanh ζ (3.926602). The arithmetic slip seems to propagate: next page's sound number 4.9079 matches 3.92666²/π = 4.90791, whereas the correct value is 3.92660²/π ≈ 4.9078.
Calling ζ = 0 the 'status aequilibrii' is slightly loose. For a free–pinned beam it is a genuine zero-frequency rigid-body rotation about B, not merely the trivial solution.
Negligible: the higher roots are truncated rather than rounded (e.g. 13π/4 = 10.2101761 is printed 10.21017). Neglecting ω for n ≥ 2 is justified, since e^{−9π/2} ≈ 7·10^{−7}.

ideas.what: Frequency equation tan ζ = tanh ζ for the free–pinned (equivalently clamped–pinned) beam, with numerical roots
ideas.modern_name: Characteristic equation of the Euler–Bernoulli beam with free/clamped–pinned boundary conditions
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E443; earlier beam work in E40 / Additamentum to the Methodus inveniendi) and Daniel Bernoulli; tabulated later by Rayleigh and others
ideas.where_published: E443, Novi Commentarii Acad. Petrop. 17 (1773); Truesdell's 'Rational mechanics of flexible or elastic bodies' (Opera omnia II.11.2) discusses Euler's beam frequencies

ideas.what: Asymptotic location of the roots at (4n+1)π/4 with exponentially small correction ω ≈ e^{−(4n+1)π/2}, refined by fixed-point iteration
ideas.modern_name: Asymptotic expansion / fixed-point iteration for transcendental eigenvalue equations
ideas.usually_credited_to: Standard technique; Euler used it similarly for other beam cases
ideas.where_published: E443 and Euler's earlier elastic-lamina papers (e.g. E40 appendix on elastic curves)

ideas.what: Symmetry ζ → −ζ of the frequency equation, so negative roots give the same eigenvalues

deep.surprise_reason: This is a standard, correct derivation of the free–pinned beam eigenvalues with a nice exponentially small correction. Its only notable feature is a minor numerical slip (3.92666 for 3.92660) that propagates into the next page's sound number. Nothing here is absent from the historical record.
transcription_corrections: The symbol written ϱ (rho) denotes a right angle, π/2 (5/2 ϱ = 3.927), not π. The same holds for 'ρ' in e^{2ζ} = Tang(½ρ + ζ) on the previous page.
The image confirms the printed value '3,92666' (an Euler/typesetting slip; the correct value is 3,92660), so the transcription is faithful here.
